name: Deep Lake
license: Apache 2.0 since version 4.0 (October 2024); Mozilla Public License 2.0 for 3.x and earlier. The hosted Activeloop service is commercial
summary: Activeloop’s storage format and database for AI data: images, video, audio, text and embeddings stored as compressed columns on object storage, searchable by vector and streamable straight into PyTorch or TensorFlow.
intro: Deep Lake stores a dataset as columns of tensors, chunked and compressed, on S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure, any S3-compatible store such as MinIO, local disk or Activeloop’s own cloud. Images, audio and video can stay in their native compression (JPEG, MP3, MP4) inside the chunks, next to labels, annotations, text and embeddings. The library is a client: it reads only the chunks a query or training loop needs, so there is no server to run for the open-source version. It versions data like Git, with commits and branches, and its dataloaders stream batches over the network into PyTorch and TensorFlow while a model trains. A query language, TQL, filters, joins and runs vector similarity search over a dataset, and LangChain and LlamaIndex use Deep Lake as a vector store for retrieval-augmented generation.

Version 4.0 (October 2024) moved the core to C++, added eventual consistency for concurrent writers, broke API compatibility with 3.x and switched the licence to Apache 2.0. The repository now also contains `pg_deeplake`, a PostgreSQL extension that adds a `deeplake` table access method and index for vector, BM25 full-text and hybrid search. Activeloop markets the hosted product as a GPU-native database for AI agents, alongside Postgres and DuckDB; packages on PyPI kept coming through August 2026 (4.7.4), while the last commit to the public GitHub repository was in May 2026.
strengths: Keeps raw media and its embeddings, labels and metadata in one dataset, instead of a vector database plus a separate file store
Serverless by design: the open-source library works directly against your own bucket, with nothing to deploy
Streams training data to PyTorch and TensorFlow and versions datasets with commits and branches
Ready integrations as a vector store in LangChain and LlamaIndex
limits: Two incompatible generations: 4.x changed the API and format, so 3.x code and datasets need converting
All computation runs in the client, so query speed depends on the client’s connection to object storage
Activeloop’s focus has moved to its hosted GPU database, and the open repository has fallen behind the PyPI releases
A smaller ecosystem than general vector databases or table formats like Lance, Iceberg or Delta Lake

story: Training deep learning models means moving millions of images, videos and audio clips from cloud storage to GPUs fast enough to keep them busy. Data lakes built for tables, with Parquet files and SQL engines, were not designed for tensors and raw media. Activeloop published its first open-source library for this, `hub`, on PyPI in August 2019: datasets stored as chunked arrays in object storage that train code could index like NumPy arrays and stream from the cloud.

In 2022 the project took the name Deep Lake, and a paper by Davit Buniatyan and the Activeloop team described it as a lakehouse for deep learning, with time travel, a Tensor Query Language, in-browser visualization and streaming to PyTorch, TensorFlow and JAX. LangChain and LlamaIndex later added it as a vector store for LLM apps. Version 4.0 in October 2024 rewrote the core in C++ and moved to Apache 2.0; by 2026 Activeloop was selling a hosted, GPU-native database for AI agents built on the format.

choices.choice: Store data as compressed tensor chunks
choices.why: Training reads samples in batches, and media is already compressed; chunking arrays and keeping native compression lets a dataloader fetch exactly the bytes a batch needs without decoding whole files.

choices.choice: Compute in the client, not a server
choices.why: Data already sits in the team’s own bucket, so a library that reads it directly avoids running and paying for a database server, and works the same locally and in any cloud.
Models are only reproducible if you know which version of the data they saw, so datasets get commits, branches and diffs.
